How to write one of these on a test

A proof here is a short chain of equal signs (or one comparison) where every link has a reason. The proofs your instructor described are four to six lines long. The same four moves work for all of them:

  1. Write what you are given and what you must show. One line each. It tells the marker, and you, where the chain starts and where it has to end.
  2. Start from a definition or from one side. Write the definition of the thing on the left (, , , "independent") and work toward the other side. Do not start from the statement you are proving.
  3. Change one thing per line and name the rule. "Definition of ", "Axiom 3, disjoint", " and independent", "a pmf sums to 1". The reason is what earns the mark.
  4. Finish with a sentence. "So and are independent." "So this is not a pmf."
Show that … = …Start at one side, end at the other. Most of this page.
Is it …? Justify.Compute both sides of the test (product rule, the two pmf conditions), compare, and state the verdict.
Is it necessarily true?To prove yes, argue for every case. To prove no, one counterexample is enough.

So the events are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.

2.5.12

The probability that at least one of several independent events occurs

Devore Supplementary Exercise 107, p. 94Standard

A subject gets a sequence of glimpses to detect a target. Let be the event that the target is detected on the th glimpse, with , and suppose the are independent. Write an expression for the probability that the target has been detected by the end of the th glimpse, and justify each step.

Hint. "Detected by the end of the th glimpse" means at least one of occurs. Work with the complement: none of them occurs.

Model proof each line on the left, the reason on the right

  1. detected means at least one occurs
  2. complement rule
  3. De Morgan's law: not detected means missed every time
  4. independent events stay independent when replaced by their complements (p. 88)
  5. complement rule on each factor

This "one minus the product of the misses" pattern is the standard route for any "at least one" question with independent events.

What a typical exam question looks like

Going by what was said in class about Term Test I (short written justifications, like Tutorial 4 question 2, at the level of the computing formula for ), expect one of these shapes:

  • "Show that …" an identity with sums or probabilities, four to six lines. Examples: the computing formula, , .
  • "If and are independent, show that … are independent." The three complement versions in §2.5.
  • "Are these events independent? Justify." From a two-dice grid or from given probabilities. Count or compute, compare with , and write the verdict.
  • "Is this a legitimate pmf? Justify." or "find ". Check both conditions.
  • "Is it necessarily true that …?" A reason if yes, one counterexample if no.

This is a guide to the style, not a prediction of the questions. Tutorial 4 itself was not among the files used to build this page, so the three complement proofs in §2.5 are the textbook's versions of its question 2.
